# Teasel Lock Keeper's Handbook

## Working the lock

- The Teasel lock is worked by the keeper alone from seven in the morning, and a boat is let through only when the lock is full on its own side and the gates are shut behind it. The keeper opens the bottom paddles before the top paddles when emptying and never the reverse, as a rush from the top paddles into a nearly empty chamber swings a narrowboat across the cill. A boat that grounds on the cill is lifted off by letting a little water back in, never hauled off by the rope, and the keeper writes the boat's name and number in the lock book with the time for the toll clerk.
- The Teasel lock lifts boats 2.6 metres and takes 11 minutes to fill from empty with both top paddles fully drawn, a time the keeper checks against the clock over the door on the first boat of the day. If the fill takes longer than fourteen minutes the keeper looks for a blocked culvert or a ground paddle that has not drawn fully, and reports a slow lock to the district office at the end of the day. Water is precious in summer, so a keeper who sees two boats approaching from opposite sides waits and lets them both pass in a single fill.
- The towpath bridge below the lock is raised for any boat with a mast, and the keeper winds the bridge by the long handle kept in the keeper's hut. Cyclists and walkers are held back behind the white line painted on the path while the bridge is up, and the keeper calls out to warn them. The bridge may not be wound while a horse is on it, and horse-drawn boats must stop at the white post 50 metres short and unhitch the horse before the tow rope is passed under the bridge.
- Tolls at Teasel are paid in the hut window and the keeper issues a numbered ticket from the book for every boat. The toll is set by the length of the boat, and a narrowboat of 60 feet pays 3 shillings each way, which the keeper writes on the ticket and the stub. Boats without a ticket for the stretch above the lock are stopped by the next keeper up the cut and sent back to Teasel to pay, and a boatman who is stopped twice in a season has his licence marked in the register by the company agent.
- The lock gates are greased at the heel posts every Monday with the tallow pot from the hut, and the keeper inspects the gate balance beams for rot with the spike at the same time. A beam that gives to the spike more than a fingertip is condemned and the gate chained shut until the carpenter comes from the yard at Wick, usually within three days. The lock is shut to traffic during the carpenter's visit and a notice is nailed to the gate post, and boats are asked to moor above and wait their turn.
